passage: At the small bank branch in Sirsa, Vishal noticed how often Irfan's phone buzzed at lunch, and how his shoulders dropped each time. Once Irfan read a message aloud with a laugh: "Useless as always, can't even buy the right rice." "That's just her way," he said. "She's stressed." Vishal had heard "just her way" many times now: about the shouting in front of guests, about the jokes at his expense in front of her family. He wanted to argue, to list every example. Instead, walking to the bus stand that evening, he said once, quietly, "Irfan, the way she talks to you sounds hurtful to me. You deserve respect. I'm around, any time." Irfan didn't answer. But the next week, he asked Vishal to have chai after work.

qa.q: What did the message Irfan read aloud say?
qa.a: "Useless as always, can't even buy the right rice."

qa.q: What did Vishal feel hearing "just her way" again?
qa.a: He felt worried and frustrated, tempted to argue with a list of examples, but chose to hold back.

qa.q: Why was Vishal's approach wise?
qa.a: He named it gently once, said Irfan deserves respect, and offered to be around, which keeps the door open instead of making Irfan defend his partner.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt hearing Vishal's words?
qa.a: Perhaps uncomfortable and quiet at first, but also seen; asking for chai the next week suggests he felt he had someone safe to talk to.

grounding: A friend notices a colleague excusing repeated disrespect from his partner, names it gently once and stays available.

passage: Gurpreet, you're scared of reading aloud in class? Let me tell you about your Joseph grandpa at nine. But every time a teacher said, "Joseph, stand up," my whole body jumped and my voice went small. My mother noticed and asked my sister. She told us: my voice had cracked on the high note, the whole school laughed, and I ran off the stage. I still don't remember it. But my body did. Knowing helped, beta. passage: In the hospital room in Pune, Rukmini placed her newborn daughter in her sister Aditi's arms. The baby's tiny fist closed around Aditi's finger. passage: The monsoon bus was packed and dripping, and Zeenat was holding her brand-new blue school bag high above the puddles on the floor. Sumit, squashed against the window, watched it. It had a zip pocket for pencils and a picture of a tiger. His own bag had a broken strap tied with string. "Showing off again," he muttered loudly to the boy next to him. "She thinks she's better than everyone. She's jealous of all of us." Zeenat went pink and lowered the bag. At home, Sumit threw his own bag into a corner. His grandmother picked it up, looked at the string, and then at him. "Is it Zeenat who's jealous, or somebody else?" Sumit stared at the floor for a long time.

qa.q: What picture was on Zeenat's bag?
qa.a: A tiger.

qa.q: Why did Sumit say Zeenat was jealous of everyone?
qa.a: He envied her new bag compared with his broken one, and putting the jealousy on her hid his own uncomfortable feeling.

qa.q: What could Sumit do next?
qa.a: Admit, at least to his grandmother, that he wishes he had a bag like that, and be kinder to Zeenat tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Zeenat react to Sumit's comment?
qa.a: She went pink and lowered the bag, likely feeling embarrassed and hurt.

grounding: A child who envies a classmate's new bag accuses her of showing off and being jealous.

subtype: Accusing a friend of the child's own envy [Actor]
passage: On the first day after the Christmas holidays, Chetan walked through the Bengaluru school gate with a shiny new cricket kit bag, zips everywhere. A crowd gathered. Kavitha stood at the edge. "He's just showing off," she told her friends at lunch. "He's jealous of everyone who plays better than him. That's why he got it." She said it three times. In the evening her mother heard her going on about Chetan again. "You've mentioned his bag six times, Kavitha," she said gently. "Do you wish you had one?" Kavitha opened her mouth to say no, then burst into tears. "I've wanted one forever."

qa.q: What did Chetan bring on the first day after the holidays?
qa.a: A shiny new cricket kit bag with zips everywhere.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha burst into tears?
qa.a: Her mother's question uncovered the envy she had been placing on Chetan; she felt sad and exposed about wanting a kit bag forever.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's mother help?
qa.a: She noticed the repetition and gently asked whether Kavitha wished she had one, making it safe to own the feeling.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel if he hears what Kavitha said?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since he was simply excited about his new bag.

grounding: A child who envies a classmate's new kit bag accuses him of showing off and jealousy.

passage: On the first day with his new thick-framed glasses, Yusuf walked into Class 10 sure that everyone was staring. When two girls at the back laughed, he knew it was about him. When the teacher glanced his way, he saw pity. He kept his head down all day and didn't raise his hand once. At lunch, Bhavna sat beside him. "Nice glasses. Did you get them at the shop near the station?" Yusuf flinched, waiting for the joke. It didn't come. "The girls at the back were laughing at a meme," she added, "not you." Yusuf looked up for the first time that day. The voice saying "you look ridiculous" had been his own.

qa.q: What did Bhavna say the girls at the back were laughing at?
qa.a: A meme, not Yusuf.

qa.q: Why was Yusuf sure everyone was staring?
qa.a: He felt insecure about his new glasses, and his own self-criticism made ordinary laughs and glances feel like contempt.

qa.q: What could help Yusuf the next time he feels judged?
qa.a: Checking the facts, as Bhavna did, and noticing when the harsh voice is his own rather than other people's.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Yusuf that day?
qa.a: She seems to notice he is withdrawn and wants to reassure him, and genuinely likes the glasses.

grounding: A teenager insecure about new glasses feels the whole class is judging him, though the harsh voice is his own.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
You asked why I didn't want to come to the Christmas youth fellowship. Honestly, it's my skin. This month it's been really bad, and I'm sure every person in church stares at it. When the choir leader looked at me during practice, I thought, she thinks I'm disgusting. When two boys whispered, I knew it was about me. Then yesterday my friend said, "You're so quiet lately, is something wrong?" Nobody had even mentioned my face. I think the only one saying mean things about my skin is me. It's strange how loud my own voice sounds when it pretends to be everyone else's. Maybe I'll come on Sunday.
Lalremsiami

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami's friend ask?
qa.a: "You're so quiet lately, is something wrong?"

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami think the choir leader found her skin disgusting?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt ashamed of the skin, and that harsh self-criticism made the leader's glance feel like contempt.

qa.q: What might help Lalremsiami go on Sunday?
qa.a: Remembering that nobody actually mentioned the skin, and testing fears against what people really say, perhaps by talking with Jeevan or the friend.

qa.q: How might the friend feel noticing Lalremsiami's quietness?
qa.a: Concerned and caring, wondering what is wrong rather than judging anyone's looks.

grounding: A teenager unsure about their skin feels everyone at church is judging, then realises the criticism is their own.

passage: You want the embarrassing story, Eshaan? Fine. I'm Maria, and in Year 9 I shot up, suddenly taller than every boy in class. I became convinced the whole school was mocking me. If someone laughed in the corridor, it was about my height. If the PE teacher smiled, it was pity. I started slouching so hard my back hurt. Then one day a girl I barely knew told me, "I always wanted to be tall like you." I actually thought she was being sarcastic! It took me months to realise that the cruel commentary running in my head all day was mine. Nobody else was saying it. I was saying it, and hearing it in everyone's voice.

qa.q: Who did Maria become taller than in Year 9?
qa.a: Every boy in class.

qa.q: Why did Maria think the girl was being sarcastic?
qa.a: Maria felt so insecure about height that even a compliment sounded like mockery; the self-criticism coloured everything.

qa.q: What could help a teenager in Maria's position sooner?
qa.a: Talking to someone trusted and checking the evidence: who has actually said anything unkind? Often no one has.

qa.q: How might the girl who complimented Maria feel if she knew it was taken as sarcasm?
qa.a: Surprised and a little sad, since she meant it sincerely.

grounding: A teenager insecure about their height feels the whole school is mocking, then realises the criticism was their own.

subtype: Being accused of hostility one does not feel [Receiver]
passage: It was the night before Tanuja's final exam, the power had gone out, and she was revising by phone torch at the kitchen table when her flatmate Nitin walked in. "You know what, Tanuja? You've been cold to me for weeks. You're secretly angry. Just admit it." Tanuja blinked. She wasn't angry; she was tired. Her first instinct was to apologise for something she hadn't done. Instead she took a breath. "I don't feel angry. Can you tell me what I did?" Nitin listed: she hadn't come to his birthday dinner, she didn't laugh at his joke. "The dinner was the night of my practical," she said calmly. "And I'm not cold. I'm stressed." Nitin paused. Then, quietly: "Maybe I'm still upset you got the bigger room."

qa.q: What was Tanuja doing when Nitin walked in?
qa.a: Revising by phone torch at the kitchen table.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel when accused of being secretly angry?
qa.a: Surprised and tired, with an urge to apologise, but she stayed steady because she knew she wasn't angry.

qa.q: How did Tanuja avoid taking on the charge?
qa.a: She took a breath, said she didn't feel angry, asked for specifics, and calmly checked each one against the facts.

qa.q: What seems really to be going on for Nitin?
qa.a: He seems to be the one holding a grudge about the bigger room, and saw his own resentment in Tanuja.

grounding: A student accused of hidden anger calmly checks the facts, and the flatmate's own grudge comes to light.

subtype: Being accused of hostility one does not feel [Receiver]
passage: In their shared flat in Delhi, Parul set her cup down hard on the counter. "Gautam, you've been passive-aggressive all week. I can feel you judging me." Gautam, washing dishes, felt his stomach drop. Had he been? He thought back carefully. He'd been quiet, yes, because of his internship interviews. He hadn't said anything about her. But he remembered she had been furious last month when he forgot to pay his share of the wifi, and she had never quite let it go. "I don't think I've been judging you," he said slowly. "Can you give me an example?" She couldn't, quite. "You just seem cold." "I've been nervous about interviews," he said. "Is anything still bothering you about the wifi?" Parul looked away.

qa.q: What had Gautam forgotten to pay last month?
qa.a: His share of the wifi.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when Parul accused him?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he felt anxious and briefly doubted himself, then steadied by checking his memory.

qa.q: What did Gautam do instead of apologising or arguing?
qa.a: He reviewed the facts, asked for an example, explained his interview nerves, and gently asked whether the wifi issue still bothered her.

qa.q: What might Parul be feeling when she looks away?
qa.a: Perhaps caught out and a bit embarrassed, sensing that her own leftover irritation was what she felt in him.

grounding: A student accused of being cold checks the facts calmly, and the flatmate's old grudge surfaces.

"You're angry at me, Tushar. I can tell."

Asif was silent. Then: "You didn't back me up when the others wanted to leave early."
"Ah. That I didn't know. Let's talk about it."

qa.q: How did Tushar handle the accusation?
qa.a: He checked each claim against the facts, said he wasn't angry, and then asked whether Asif was upset, which revealed the real issue.

qa.q: What was Asif actually feeling?
